overview: Later Jin was the northern Chinese dynasty founded by Shi Jingtang in 936 and conquered by the Khitan in 947. Its court ruled from Kaifeng during the turbulent Five Dynasties era. This is a separate state from ancient Jin and the later Jurchen Jin. The atlas dates fit its historical lifespan, but its polygon is a coarse illustration of the northern realm, not a precise record of changing control.

periods.title: Shi Jingtang’s reign
periods.summary: The founder establishes a new imperial court; his reign ends with his death in 942.

periods.title: Shi Chonggui’s reign
periods.summary: The second ruler succeeds in 942. Khitan conquest ends the dynasty in early 947.

sections.title: An imperial court with a powerful neighbour

items.text: Shi Jingtang had commanded a frontier region for Later Tang. Khitan military help enabled him to found Later Jin, but the alliance had a heavy price: he ceded sixteen northern prefectures. His new dynasty therefore began with a powerful neighbour controlling territory that earlier northern Chinese courts had held.

The border bargain outlived Later Jin. Song emperors later tried repeatedly to recover the lost prefectures without lasting success. A decision made to secure one ruler’s throne shaped the strategic problems of later dynasties. The atlas excludes these prefectures in its approximate Later Jin outline.

Shi Chonggui was Shi Jingtang’s nephew and adopted son. The later New History describes officials placing him on the throne when the founder died in 942. Succession was a family matter with enormous public consequences: a child’s position in the imperial household could affect who commanded armies and appointed officials.

sections.title: Food, family visits and the government’s demands

items.text: In 940, the court ordered public and private debts outstanding through the end of 938 to be cancelled. The Old History preserves the decree. It reveals a government trying to relieve old obligations, although the order alone cannot tell us how successfully each household obtained relief.

Officials visiting their parents received gifts of tea and medicines under an order of 940. The court explicitly followed an earlier precedent. Family duties and official employment overlapped: a trip home could come with useful supplies for the visit.

The same year, Shi Jingtang stopped deliveries of garden melons and fruit from Luoyang and Jingzhao. The stated reason was concern for the people doing the work. A ruler’s fruit bowl had a transport bill, paid partly in other people’s labour.

Locusts threatened food supplies in 943. The New History records soldiers being sent to catch them and civilians offered grain for collecting them. Fighting a harvest-eating swarm required hands as well as orders; the same annals also describe coercive grain requisitions during this difficult year.

Shi Jingtang enjoyed explanations of the Daodejing by the Daoist Zhang Jianming. In 940 he ordered its two parts carved onto printing blocks, with a new preface by He Ning, for distribution. A conversation at court could lead to a much larger copying project.

The work now called the Old Book of Tang was completed in 945 under Later Jin. Its 200 chapters drew on records available relatively soon after Tang’s fall. Preserving the previous dynasty’s history became one of this short-lived court’s most durable achievements: later readers could study events far beyond their own memories.

The National Museum of China preserves a Later Jin Tianfu Yuanbao coin measuring 2.2 centimetres across. Its description explains that new dynastic coins circulated alongside older Tang money. A change of emperor did not mean everyone immediately emptied their purse and replaced every coin.

sections.title: Rooms, objects and hopes preserved underground

items.text: A tomb excavated at Jinci in 2005 belonged to Lady Wang and dates to 937. Its brick chamber imitates a timber building, with painted pillars, doors and windows. Craftspeople created an architectural setting underground, leaving details of construction and decoration that real wooden rooms often lose.

Lady Wang’s grave contained ceramic vessels, a bronze mirror, hairpins, thirteen Kaiyuan coins and an iron ploughshare. The surprising mix brings grooming, containers, money and farming tools together in a burial. The official Guo Zhimi arranged it, but the inscription does not identify his relationship to her.

The 937 epitaph includes 子孫興盛，諸災永息, rendered here in modern traditional type. Modern Mandarin reads zǐ sūn xīng shèng, zhū zāi yǒng xī: “May descendants flourish; may all calamities cease.” This translated wish comes from a burial invocation. The carved text is contemporary, while the typeface and pronunciation guide are modern.

Dayunyuan monastery at Pingshun was founded in 938, initially under another name. Its surviving Amitabha hall belongs to the Five Dynasties period, while much of the complex is later. Inside are period murals with richly coloured lines and raised gilded details. Worshippers encountered skilled woodworking and painting together; the surviving hall preserves a rare part of that setting.

After the conquest, the captive imperial family was sent north. The New History lists a physician, seven cooks and tea-and-wine attendants among its reduced household, yet later describes hardship and gathering wild plants for food. These are the experiences of a displaced royal group, whose former rank no longer guaranteed comfort.

ending.text: The Khitan destroyed Later Jin after its field army surrendered and Kaifeng fell in early 947. Shi Chonggui survived as a captive. This ended the dynasty, not the lives of its population or the circulation of its books and coins.
